subject: psychology
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: In the Ponzo illusion, the upper line looks longer because of which cue being misapplied?
questions.explain: The Ponzo illusion uses linear perspective cues that make the upper of two equal lines seem longer.

questions.q: The Kanizsa triangle, where we 'see' edges that are not there, is which type of illusion?
questions.explain: The Kanizsa triangle is a fiction illusion: we perceive contours and a shape that do not physically exist.

questions.q: In Gibson's theory, the apparent movement of objects as we move is called what?
questions.explain: Optic flow is the pattern of apparent movement Gibson said gives direct information about depth and motion.

questions.q: Gibson's direct theory of perception is best described as which type of processing?
questions.explain: Gibson's direct theory is bottom-up: perception comes directly from rich information in the visual environment.

questions.q: In the Ames room, why does one person appear far larger than the other?
options: The room's distorted shape is misperceived as a normal rectangular room
questions.explain: The Ames room is distorted but seen as normal, so people at different distances appear very different in size.

questions.q: Objects that overlap others appear closer. This monocular depth cue is called what?
questions.explain: Superimposition (overlap) is a monocular cue: a partly hidden object is seen as further away.

questions.q: The finding that people from different cultures fall for illusions differently suggests what affects perception?
questions.explain: Cultural differences in susceptibility to illusions show that experience and environment shape perception.

questions.q: In the texture gradient cue, surfaces look further away when their texture appears how?
questions.explain: Texture gradient is a monocular cue: texture looks finer and denser as a surface recedes into the distance.

questions.q: Gilchrist and Nesberg's study, where hungry participants saw food images as brighter, shows the effect of what?
questions.explain: It shows that motivation, such as hunger, can influence and bias perception of relevant stimuli.

questions.q: The Necker cube and Rubin's vase are examples of which type of illusion?
questions.explain: These are ambiguous figures that can be perceived in more than one way and seem to 'flip'.

questions.q: Which of these is a BINOCULAR depth cue?
questions.explain: Retinal disparity is binocular: the slight difference between the two eyes' images signals depth.

questions.q: Hungry people identifying more food-related images shows which influence on perception?
questions.explain: Motivation and emotion, such as hunger, can bias perception towards relevant stimuli.

questions.q: Which theory would best explain how we still recognise a familiar object seen in poor lighting using prior knowledge?
questions.explain: Gregory's top-down theory uses prior knowledge and inference to interpret incomplete or poor visual input.

questions.q: Which of these is a MONOCULAR depth cue (needing only one eye)?
questions.explain: Relative size is a monocular cue; smaller images are perceived as further away, using only one eye.

questions.q: Expecting to see something can make you misread it. This shows the effect of what on perception?
questions.explain: Expectation, or perceptual set, can lead us to perceive what we anticipate rather than what is actually there.

questions.q: The fact that people raised in 'carpentered' (right-angled) environments are more fooled by the Muller-Lyer illusion suggests perception is shaped by what?
questions.explain: This finding suggests that the environment and culture we grow up in shape how we perceive illusions.

questions.q: One criticism of Gregory's constructivist theory is that it struggles to explain what?
options: Why perception is usually accurate despite relying on guesses
questions.explain: If perception is just inference, it is hard to explain why our everyday perception is usually so accurate.

questions.q: Gregory's constructivist theory argues perception is mainly what?
options: Built top-down using prior knowledge and expectation
A direct readout of the world
questions.explain: Gregory argued perception is constructed top-down, using prior knowledge, inference and expectation.

questions.q: The binocular cue based on the eyes turning inwards to focus on a near object is called what?
questions.explain: Convergence is a binocular cue: the inward turn of the eyes signals how near an object is.

questions.q: Bruner and Minturn's study, where a figure was read as 'B' or '13' depending on context, demonstrates what?
options: The effect of context/expectation on perception
questions.explain: It shows perceptual set: surrounding context shapes how an ambiguous stimulus is perceived.

questions.q: Perceptual set is best defined as what?
options: A tendency to perceive some things and ignore others based on expectation
questions.explain: Perceptual set is a readiness to perceive certain features, shaped by expectation, context, culture and emotion.

questions.q: As parallel lines (such as railway tracks) appear to meet in the distance, this monocular cue is called what?
questions.explain: Linear perspective is a monocular cue where parallel lines seem to converge with distance.
